claim: XAB2 is involved specifically and exclusively in Transcription-Coupled Nucleotide Excision Repair (TC-NER) reactions.
source: In this study, we demonstrate that XAB2 is involved specifically and exclusively in Transcription-Coupled Nucleotide Excision Repair (TC-NER) reactions and solely for RNA polymerase 2 (RNAP2)-transcribed genes.
evidence: Supported by TCR-UDS assay data showing decreased repair replication in XAB2-silenced cells (Figure 1D), and RRS assay showing no restart of transcription after UV damage in XAB2-silenced cells (Figure 1C).

claim: XAB2 is involved solely for RNA polymerase 2 (RNAP2)-transcribed genes.
source: In this study, we demonstrate that XAB2 is involved specifically and exclusively in Transcription-Coupled Nucleotide Excision Repair (TC-NER) reactions and solely for RNA polymerase 2 (RNAP2)-transcribed genes.
evidence: Supported by RNA-FISH data showing that RNAP1 transcription restarts after UV irradiation in XAB2-silenced cells (Figure 2—figure supplement 2B), indicating XAB2 is not required for repair of RNAP1-transcribed genes.

claim: XAB2 does not accumulate on local UV-C damage.
source: Surprisingly, contrary to all the other NER proteins studied so far, XAB2 does not accumulate on the local UV-C damage; on the contrary, it becomes more mobile after damage induction.
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence data showing release of XAB2 from damaged areas (Figure 3A, B) and FRAP experiments showing increased XAB2 mobility after UV irradiation (Figure 4A).

claim: XAB2 becomes more mobile after damage induction.
source: Surprisingly, contrary to all the other NER proteins studied so far, XAB2 does not accumulate on the local UV-C damage; on the contrary, it becomes more mobile after damage induction.
evidence: Supported by FRAP experiments showing dose-dependent increase in XAB2 mobility after UV irradiation (Figure 4A).

claim: XAB2 mobility is restored when DNA repair reactions are completed.
source: XAB2 mobility is restored when DNA repair reactions are completed.
evidence: Supported by FRAP data showing recovery of intrinsic XAB2 mobility 16 hr post-irradiation in wild-type cells (Figure 4A), which correlates with completion of repair and restart of transcription.

claim: XAB2 is detached after DNA damage induction from DNA:RNA hybrids (R-loops).
source: By scrutinizing from which cellular complex/partner/structure XAB2 is released, we have identified that XAB2 is detached after DNA damage induction from DNA:RNA hybrids, commonly known as R-loops, and from the CSA and XPG proteins.
evidence: Supported by PLA experiments showing reduced interaction between XAB2 and R-loops after UV irradiation (Figure 5D).

claim: XAB2 is detached after DNA damage induction from CSA protein.
source: By scrutinizing from which cellular complex/partner/structure XAB2 is released, we have identified that XAB2 is detached after DNA damage induction from DNA:RNA hybrids, commonly known as R-loops, and from the CSA and XPG proteins.
evidence: Supported by PLA experiments showing clear and consistent release from CSA protein 2 hr after UV irradiation (Figure 6A).

claim: XAB2 is detached after DNA damage induction from XPG protein.
source: By scrutinizing from which cellular complex/partner/structure XAB2 is released, we have identified that XAB2 is detached after DNA damage induction from DNA:RNA hybrids, commonly known as R-loops, and from the CSA and XPG proteins.
evidence: Supported by PLA experiments showing clear and consistent release from XPG protein 1 hr after UV irradiation (Figure 6C).

claim: XAB2 release contributes to the DNA damage recognition step during TC-NER.
source: This release contributes to the DNA damage recognition step during TC-NER, as in the absence of XAB2, RNAP2 is blocked longer on UV lesions.
evidence: Supported by PLA experiments showing stronger and more persistent interaction of RNAP2 with 6-4PP lesions in XAB2-silenced cells (Figure 7B).

claim: In the absence of XAB2, RNAP2 is blocked longer on UV lesions.
source: This release contributes to the DNA damage recognition step during TC-NER, as in the absence of XAB2, RNAP2 is blocked longer on UV lesions.
evidence: Supported by PLA experiments showing stronger and more persistent interaction of RNAP2 with 6-4PP lesions after UV irradiation in XAB2-silenced cells (Figure 7B).

claim: XAB2 has a role in retaining RNAP2 on its substrate without any DNA damage.
source: Moreover, we also demonstrate that XAB2 has a role in retaining RNAP2 on its substrate without any DNA damage.
evidence: Supported by FRAP experiments showing that depletion of XAB2 significantly increased the mobility of RNAP2 (Figure 7A).

claim: XAB2 is not involved in the GG-NER subpathway.
source: This result shows that XAB2 is not involved in the GG-NER subpathway, but does not exclude an involvement of XAB2 in the TC-NER subpathway.
evidence: Supported by UDS assay showing no decreased level of UDS in XAB2-silenced cells (Figure 1A).

claim: No restart of transcription after UV damage was observed in XAB2-silenced cells.
source: In XAB2-silenced cells, no restart of transcription after UV damage was observed (Figure 1C, blue column and Figure 1—figure supplement 2A), as well as in siXPF-treated cells due to the inability to repair DNA lesions (Figure 1C, red column and Figure 2—figure supplement 2A) and in contrast with siMock-treated cells (Figure 1C, black column and Figure 1—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: Supported by RRS assay data showing no recovery of RNA synthesis 16-24 hr after UV irradiation in XAB2-silenced cells (Figure 1C).

claim: Silencing of XAB2 results in a decrease in TCR-UDS levels.
source: Silencing of XAB2 results in a decrease in TCR-UDS levels (Figure 1D, blue column and Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
evidence: Supported by TCR-UDS assay data in GG-NER-deficient cells showing decreased repair replication in XAB2-silenced cells (Figure 1D).

claim: XAB2 interacts with 6-4PP lesions 1 hr after UV irradiation.
source: We observed a strong interaction between XAB2 and 6-4PPs 1 hr after 10 J/m² irradiation (Figure 2A, C).
evidence: Supported by PLA experiments showing strong interaction between XAB2 and 6-4PPs 1 hr after irradiation (Figure 2A, C).

claim: The interaction between XAB2 and 6-4PPs decreases during repair.
source: This interaction correlates with the amount of 6-4PPs and, as expected, decreases during repair (Figure 2B, C), while XAB2 concentration does not change after irradiation (Figure 2B, C).
evidence: Supported by PLA and IF data showing decreased XAB2-6-4PP interaction over time while XAB2 levels remain constant (Figure 2B, C).

claim: XAB2 concentration does not change after irradiation.
source: This interaction correlates with the amount of 6-4PPs and, as expected, decreases during repair (Figure 2B, C), while XAB2 concentration does not change after irradiation (Figure 2B, C).
evidence: Supported by IF data showing constant XAB2 levels at different time points after UV irradiation (Figure 2B, C).

claim: XAB2 interacts with CPD lesions.
source: The same result is obtained in PLA experiment between XAB2 and CPDs (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by PLA experiments showing interaction between XAB2 and CPDs (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).

claim: RNAP1 transcription restarts after irradiation in the absence of XAB2.
source: In the absence of XAB2, 40 hr after irradiation, the level of 47S returns to the level of non-irradiated condition, supporting a restart of RNAP1 transcription (Figure 2—figure supplement 2B, blue column and Figure 2—figure supplement 2D).
evidence: Supported by RNA-FISH data showing recovery of 47S pre-rRNA levels 40 hr after UV irradiation in XAB2-silenced cells (Figure 2—figure supplement 2B, D).

claim: XAB2, AQR, PRP19, and CCDC16 are released from the damaged area 1 hr after UV irradiation.
source: Unexpectedly, in contrast with all other NER proteins studied so far, we observed a relatively rapid (1 hr after UV irradiation) release of XAB2, AQR, PRP19, and CCDC16 from the damaged area (Figure 3A, B).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence data showing decreased signal of these proteins in locally damaged areas 1 hr after UV irradiation (Figure 3A, B).

claim: The proper localization of the XAB2-splicing complex is re-established after the completion of DNA repair reactions when the transcription is fully restarted.
source: The proper localization of the XAB2-splicing complex is re-established after the completion of DNA repair reactions when the transcription is fully restarted (16 hr after irradiation; Figure 3B).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence data showing recovery of XAB2-splicing complex localization 16 hr after UV irradiation (Figure 3B).

claim: None of the cells silenced for XAB2-related proteins (AQR, PRP19, CCDC16, PPIE, ISY1) are deficient in DNA Repair.
source: Our results clearly show that none of the cells silenced for XAB2-related proteins are deficient in DNA Repair.
evidence: Supported by UDS, TCR-UDS, and RRS assays showing proficient repair in cells silenced for AQR, PRP19, CCDC16, PPIE, or ISY1 (Figure 3—figure supplements 1–3).

claim: Both GG-NER and TC-NER are proficient in the absence of AQR, PRP19, CCDC16, PPIE, or ISY1.
source: Moreover, both GG-NER (Figure 3—figure supplement 1) and TC-NER (Figure 3—figure supplements 2 and 3) are proficient in the absence of AQR, PRP19, CCDC16, PPIE, or ISY1.
evidence: Supported by UDS and TCR-UDS assays showing normal repair levels in cells silenced for these proteins (Figure 3—figure supplements 1–3).

claim: The absence of CSA and CSB did not hinder the release of XAB2 from locally damaged areas.
source: Interestingly, the absence of CSA and CSB did not hinder the release of XAB2 from locally damaged areas.
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence data showing XAB2 release from damaged areas in CSA and CSB mutant cells (Figure 3C and Figure 3—figure supplement 4).

claim: In CSA and CSB mutant cells, XAB2 release from locally damaged areas persisted 16 hr after UV-C exposure.
source: However, this release persisted 16 hr after UV-C exposure (Figure 3C blue and red curves compared to black curve and Figure 3—figure supplement 4), suggesting that the re-establishment of the proper localization of XAB2 within the nucleus after the DNA repair process depends either on the repair process per se or on the restart of transcription after the achievement of DNA repair reactions.
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence data showing continued XAB2 release 16 hr after UV irradiation in CSA and CSB mutant cells (Figure 3C and Figure 3—figure supplement 4).

claim: XAB2 mobility increases in a dose-dependent manner after UV irradiation.
source: Interestingly, we observed a dose-dependent increase in mobility of XAB2 (Figure 4A).
evidence: Supported by FRAP experiments showing increased XAB2 mobility at different UV-C doses (2-16 J/m²) (Figure 4A).

claim: At intermediate doses of 8 J/m² of UV-C, XAB2 mobility significantly increases during repair (3 hr after UV-C exposure) and returns to normal once repair is completed (16 hr after irradiation).
source: At intermediate doses of 8 J/m² of UV-C, we observed a significant increase in XAB2 mobility during repair (3 hr after UV-C exposure) and the following return to the normal condition once the repair is completed and transcription restarted (16 hr after irradiation) (Figure 4A, green bar).
evidence: Supported by FRAP data showing transient increase in XAB2 mobility at 3 hr and recovery at 16 hr after 8 J/m² UV-C irradiation (Figure 4A).

claim: In CSA and CSB mutant cells, the increase in XAB2 mobility after 8 J/m² irradiation lasted until 24 hr after UV-C exposure.
source: Interestingly, in CSA and CSB mutant cells, the increase in XAB2 mobility is also observed after 8 J/m² irradiation and lasted until 24 hr after UV-C exposure (Figure 4B), witnessing the fact that in these cells, DNA damage is not repaired and therefore initial intrinsic XAB2 mobility is not restored.
evidence: Supported by FRAP data showing sustained increased XAB2 mobility up to 24 hr after UV irradiation in CSA and CSB mutant cells (Figure 4B).

claim: Without damage, XAB2 mobility is reduced in TC-NER-deficient cells compared to wild-type cells.
source: Interestingly, without damage, XAB2 mobility is reduced in TC-NER-deficient cells compared to wild-type cells for still unknown reasons (Figure 4B, black histogram).
evidence: Supported by FRAP data showing lower XAB2 mobility in CSA and CSB mutant cells without UV treatment (Figure 4B).

claim: XAB2 increased mobility in transcription inhibition conditions is very similar to the one measured upon UV treatment.
source: Surprisingly, results show that XAB2 increased mobility in transcription inhibition conditions is very similar to the one measured upon UV treatment (Figure 4C, red curve compared to blue curve).
evidence: Supported by FRAP data showing similar XAB2 mobility changes after DRB treatment and UV irradiation (Figure 4C).

claim: ATR and ATM inhibitors did not modify the increase of XAB2 mobility after UV irradiation.
source: Both drugs did not modify the increase of XAB2 mobility after UV irradiation (Figure 4C, green curve and Figure 4—figure supplement 1D) demonstrating that variations in XAB2 mobility after DNA damage are triggered and sustained by transcriptional inhibition.
evidence: Supported by FRAP data showing similar XAB2 mobility increase after UV irradiation in the presence of ATR or ATM inhibitors (Figure 4C and Figure 4—figure supplement 1D).

claim: Variations in XAB2 mobility after DNA damage are triggered and sustained by transcriptional inhibition.
source: Both drugs did not modify the increase of XAB2 mobility after UV irradiation (Figure 4C, green curve and Figure 4—figure supplement 1D) demonstrating that variations in XAB2 mobility after DNA damage are triggered and sustained by transcriptional inhibition.
evidence: Supported by FRAP data showing that ATR/ATM inhibitors do not prevent XAB2 mobility increase, and DRB treatment mimics UV-induced mobility changes (Figure 4C and Figure 4—figure supplement 1D).

claim: XAB2 is not released from the splicing complex during DNA repair reactions.
source: In conclusion, immunoprecipitation or PLA experiment showed that XAB2 is not released from the splicing complex during DNA repair reactions.
evidence: Supported by immunoprecipitation showing XAB2 and AQR co-immunoprecipitate after UV irradiation (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A) and PLA showing maintained or increased interaction between XAB2 and AQR after UV (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B).

claim: More XAB2 immunoprecipitated from nuclear extracts 1–3 hr after UV-C irradiation in WT cells.
source: Interestingly, while trying to immunoprecipitate XAB2 interacting partners during DNA repair reactions, we could observe that systematically and consistently, more XAB2 immunoprecipitated from nuclear extracts 1–3 hr after UV-C irradiation in WT cells (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A and Figure 5A).
evidence: Supported by immunoprecipitation data showing increased XAB2 immunoprecipitation 1-3 hr after UV irradiation (Figure 5A and Figure 5—figure supplement 1A).

claim: In CSA−/− and CSB−/− cell lines, the amount of XAB2 immunoprecipitated remained high all along the time course of the experiment (3 and 16 hr).
source: Moreover, in CSA−/− and CSB−/− cell lines, in which UV lesions on transcribed strands of genes are not repaired, the amount of XAB2 immunoprecipitated remained high all along the time course of the experiment (3 and 16 hr) (Figure 5A).
evidence: Supported by immunoprecipitation data showing sustained high levels of XAB2 immunoprecipitation in CSA and CSB mutant cells at 3 and 16 hr after UV irradiation (Figure 5A).

claim: XAB2 directly interacts with R-loops.
source: Immunoprecipitation experiments with the S9.6 antibody show that XAB2 directly interacts with R-loops (Figure 5B).
evidence: Supported by immunoprecipitation data showing XAB2 co-immunoprecipitates with R-loops using S9.6 antibody (Figure 5B).

claim: After Benzonase treatment, XAB2 is no more immunoprecipitated with R-loops.
source: Interestingly, after Benzonase treatment, XAB2 is no more immunoprecipitated (Figure 5B), suggesting that XAB2 substrate is indeed DNA:RNA hybrids.
evidence: Supported by immunoprecipitation data showing loss of XAB2 co-immunoprecipitation after Benzonase treatment which degrades DNA:RNA hybrids (Figure 5B).

claim: An increased amount of R-loops is observed in cells silenced for XAB2 or AQR compared to control cells.
source: Using this analysis method, we observed an increased amount of R-loops in cells silenced for XAB2 or AQR compared to control cells (Figure 5C and Figure 5—figure supplement 3A).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence data showing increased R-loops signal in XAB2- or AQR-silenced cells (Figure 5C and Figure 5—figure supplement 3A).

claim: After UV irradiation, there is a strong and consistent reduction of more than 40% of the interactions between R-loops and XAB2.
source: After UV irradiation, we measured a strong and consistent reduction of more than 40% of the interactions between R-loops and XAB2 and between R-loops and AQR (Figure 5D and Figure 5—figure supplement 3B).
evidence: Supported by PLA data showing >40% reduction in XAB2-R-loops interaction after UV irradiation (Figure 5D).

claim: After UV irradiation, there is a strong and consistent reduction of more than 40% of the interactions between R-loops and AQR.
source: After UV irradiation, we measured a strong and consistent reduction of more than 40% of the interactions between R-loops and XAB2 and between R-loops and AQR (Figure 5D and Figure 5—figure supplement 3B).
evidence: Supported by PLA data showing >40% reduction in AQR-R-loops interaction after UV irradiation (Figure 5D).

claim: The reduced interactions between XAB2/AQR and R-loops are not caused by a reduction in R-loops, XAB2, or AQR concentration during DNA repair.
source: These reduced interactions are not caused by a reduction in either R-loops, XAB2, or AQR concentration during DNA repair (Figure 5E and Figure 5—figure supplement 3B).
evidence: Supported by IF data showing constant levels of R-loops, XAB2, and AQR during DNA repair (Figure 5E and Figure 5—figure supplement 3B).

claim: RNAseH reduces the quantity of R-loops.
source: Our results show that RNAseH reduced the quantity of R-loops (Figure 5—figure supplement 4C,F) and in doing so, it also decreased the interaction with both XAB2 (Figure 5—figure supplement 4C, D) and AQR (Figure 5—figure supplement 4E, F).
evidence: Supported by IF and PLA data showing decreased R-loops signal after RNAseH treatment (Figure 5—figure supplement 4C, F).

claim: RNAseH decreases the interaction between R-loops and XAB2.
source: Our results show that RNAseH reduced the quantity of R-loops (Figure 5—figure supplement 4C,F) and in doing so, it also decreased the interaction with both XAB2 (Figure 5—figure supplement 4C, D) and AQR (Figure 5—figure supplement 4E, F).
evidence: Supported by PLA data showing decreased XAB2-R-loops interaction after RNAseH treatment (Figure 5—figure supplement 4C, D).

claim: RNAseH decreases the interaction between R-loops and AQR.
source: Our results show that RNAseH reduced the quantity of R-loops (Figure 5—figure supplement 4C,F) and in doing so, it also decreased the interaction with both XAB2 (Figure 5—figure supplement 4C, D) and AQR (Figure 5—figure supplement 4E, F).
evidence: Supported by PLA data showing decreased AQR-R-loops interaction after RNAseH treatment (Figure 5—figure supplement 4E, F).

claim: A reduction in the interaction between XAB2 and mRNA was observed after UV irradiation.
source: PLA results show that a reduction in the interaction between XAB2 and mRNA was observed (Figure 5—figure supplement 5A, C).
evidence: Supported by PLA data showing decreased XAB2-mRNA interaction after UV irradiation (Figure 5—figure supplement 5A, C).

claim: The reduction in XAB2-mRNA interaction paralleled the decrease of mRNA caused by UV-dependent transcription inhibition.
source: However, this reduction paralleled the decrease of mRNA caused by UV-dependent transcription inhibition (Figure 5—figure supplement 5B, C), suggesting that the results observed in the PLA XAB2-mRNAs are due mainly to a decrease in mRNAs amount (Figure 5—figure supplement 5A).
evidence: Supported by IF data showing decreased mRNA levels after UV irradiation that correlates with decreased XAB2-mRNA PLA signal (Figure 5—figure supplement 5B, C).

claim: A clear and consistent release from the CSA protein was observed 2 hr after UV irradiation.
source: Among all the proteins tested, we could observe a clear and consistent release from the CSA protein 2 hr after UV irradiation (Figure 6A) and from the XPG protein 1 hr after UV irradiation (Figure 6C).
evidence: Supported by PLA data showing reduced XAB2-CSA interaction 2 hr after UV irradiation (Figure 6A).

claim: A clear and consistent release from the XPG protein was observed 1 hr after UV irradiation.
source: Among all the proteins tested, we could observe a clear and consistent release from the CSA protein 2 hr after UV irradiation (Figure 6A) and from the XPG protein 1 hr after UV irradiation (Figure 6C).
evidence: Supported by PLA data showing reduced XAB2-XPG interaction 1 hr after UV irradiation (Figure 6C).

claim: No clear reduction of interaction was observed between XAB2 and CSB.
source: On the contrary, no clear reduction of interaction was observed between XAB2 and CSB (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A, B) or between XAB2 and XPB (Figure 6—figure supplement 1C, D).
evidence: Supported by PLA data showing no significant change in XAB2-CSB interaction after UV irradiation (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A, B).

claim: No clear reduction of interaction was observed between XAB2 and XPB.
source: On the contrary, no clear reduction of interaction was observed between XAB2 and CSB (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A, B) or between XAB2 and XPB (Figure 6—figure supplement 1C, D).
evidence: Supported by PLA data showing no significant change in XAB2-XPB interaction after UV irradiation (Figure 6—figure supplement 1C, D).

claim: Depletion of XAB2 significantly increased the mobility of RNAP2.
source: Interestingly, depletion of XAB2 significantly increased the mobility of RNAP2 (Figure 7A, dark red curve vs. dark blue curve), demonstrating that XAB2 maintains RNAP2 bound to its substrate during transcription.
evidence: Supported by FRAP data showing increased RNAP2 mobility in XAB2-silenced cells (Figure 7A).

claim: XAB2 maintains RNAP2 bound to its substrate during transcription.
source: Interestingly, depletion of XAB2 significantly increased the mobility of RNAP2 (Figure 7A, dark red curve vs. dark blue curve), demonstrating that XAB2 maintains RNAP2 bound to its substrate during transcription.
evidence: Supported by FRAP data showing increased RNAP2 mobility in XAB2-silenced cells, indicating reduced binding to substrate (Figure 7A).

claim: After UV irradiation, RNAP2 mobility did not change significantly, both in the presence and absence of XAB2.
source: Interestingly, after UV irradiation, RNAP2 mobility did not change significantly (p-value superior at 0.05), both in the presence and absence of XAB2 (Figure 7A, light curve vs. dark curve).
evidence: Supported by FRAP data showing no significant change in RNAP2 mobility after UV irradiation in either siMock or siXAB2 conditions (Figure 7A).

claim: A more robust and persistent interaction of RNAP2 with 6-4PP lesions was measured after UV irradiation in XAB2-silenced cells.
source: Remarkably, we measured a more robust and persistent interaction of RNAP2 with 6-4PP lesions after UV irradiation in XAB2-silenced cells (Figure 7B and Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by PLA data showing stronger and longer-lasting RNAP2-6-4PP interaction in XAB2-silenced cells (Figure 7B).

claim: Without XAB2, DNA is not properly repaired and as a consequence, RNAP2 interacts longer with UV lesions.
source: These results demonstrate that, without XAB2, DNA is not properly repaired and as a consequence, RNAP2 interacts longer with UV lesions.
evidence: Supported by PLA data showing stronger and more persistent RNAP2-6-4PP interaction in XAB2-silenced cells (Figure 7B), combined with TCR-UDS data showing reduced repair in XAB2-silenced cells (Figure 1D).

claim: XAB2 protein was identified as a protein interacting with XPA using a yeast two-hybrid system.
source: XAB2 protein was identified as a protein interacting with XPA, a NER factor, using a yeast two-hybrid system (Nakatsu et al., 2000).
evidence: Supported by citation to Nakatsu et al., 2000.

claim: XAB2 interacts with the TC-NER-specific factors, CSA and CSB, and the elongating form of RNAP2.
source: Next, it has been shown that XAB2 interacts also with the TC-NER-specific factors, CSA and CSB, and the elongating form of RNAP2 (Nakatsu et al., 2000).
evidence: Supported by citation to Nakatsu et al., 2000.

claim: XAB2 is essential for early mouse embryogenesis.
source: XAB2 is also essential for early mouse embryogenesis, as demonstrated by the preimplantation lethality observed in XAB2 knockout mice (Yonemasu et al., 2005).
evidence: Supported by citation to Yonemasu et al., 2005.

claim: Downregulation of XAB2 inhibits normal RNA synthesis and the recovery of RNA synthesis after UV irradiation.
source: Downregulation of XAB2, using either anti-XAB2 or siRNA, inhibits normal RNA synthesis and the recovery of RNA synthesis after UV irradiation (Kuraoka et al., 2008; Nakatsu et al., 2000).
evidence: Supported by citations to Kuraoka et al., 2008 and Nakatsu et al., 2000.

claim: Injection of anti-XAB2 in GG-NER-deficient cells significantly reduces UV-induced Unscheduled DNA Synthesis (UDS) during repair.
source: Furthermore, injection of anti-XAB2 in GG-NER-deficient cells significantly reduces UV-induced Unscheduled DNA Synthesis (UDS) during repair (Nakatsu et al., 2000).
evidence: Supported by citation to Nakatsu et al., 2000.

claim: XAB2 is a component of the Prp19/XAB2 complex required for pre-mRNA splicing.
source: Further studies have shown that XAB2 is a component of the Prp19/XAB2 complex (Aquarius [AQR], XAB2, Prp19, CCDC16, hISY1, and PPIE) or Prp19/CDC5L-related complex required for pre-mRNA splicing (Kuraoka et al., 2008).
evidence: Supported by citation to Kuraoka et al., 2008.

claim: XAB2, as well as PRP19 and AQR, has been involved in the DNA damage response (DDR).
source: XAB2, as well as PRP19 and AQR, has been involved in the DNA damage response (DDR) (Maréchal et al., 2014; Onyango et al., 2016; Sakasai et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to Maréchal et al., 2014; Onyango et al., 2016; and Sakasai et al., 2017.

claim: XAB2 is essential for homologous recombination (HR) by promoting the end resection step.
source: Indeed, XAB2 is essential for homologous recombination (HR) by promoting the end resection step (Onyango et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to Onyango et al., 2016.

claim: PRP19 is a sensor of RPA-ssDNA after DNA damage.
source: PRP19 is a sensor of RPA-ssDNA after DNA damage (Maréchal et al., 2014) and AQR contributes to the maintenance of genomic stability via regulation of HR (Sakasai et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to Maréchal et al., 2014.

claim: AQR contributes to the maintenance of genomic stability via regulation of HR.
source: PRP19 is a sensor of RPA-ssDNA after DNA damage (Maréchal et al., 2014) and AQR contributes to the maintenance of genomic stability via regulation of HR (Sakasai et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to Sakasai et al., 2017.

claim: AQR has a role in removing R-loops.
source: Interestingly, AQR has a role in removing R-loops, a three-stranded nucleic acids structure composed of a DNA:RNA hybrid and the associated nontemplate single-stranded DNA (Sollier et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to Sollier et al., 2014.

claim: R-loops are found abundantly in human gene promoters and terminators where RNA processing occurs.
source: They are found abundantly in human gene promoters and terminators where RNA processing occurs (Wang et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to Wang et al., 2018.

claim: XAB2 has been recently identified as involved in R-loops resolution.
source: Differently from total RNAs, in our study, we observe that R-loops do not decrease in number after UV damage and transcription inhibition (Figure 5E). Therefore, the interaction XAB2_R-loops and AQR_R-loops is specifically hindered after UV damage (Figure 5D). However, a careful interpretation of these results should be made because a recent paper demonstrates that the S9.6 antibody, specific for DNA:RNA hybrids, can also recognize other nucleic acid structures in immunofluorescence assay (Smolka et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citation to Goulielmaki et al., 2021 mentioned in the text.

claim: In AQR-depleted cells, R-loops formation is induced and these R-loops are actively processed into DNA double-strand breaks by XPF and XPG.
source: It was previously demonstrated that, in AQR-depleted cells, R-loops formation is induced. These R-loops are actively processed into DNA double-strand breaks by XPF and XPG, the NER endonucleases (Sollier et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to Sollier et al., 2014.

claim: A complete TC-NER mechanism is required to repair the UV lesions present on active rDNA, genes transcribed by RNAP1.
source: Previously, we reported that a complete TC-NER mechanism is required to repair the UV lesions present on active rDNA, genes transcribed by RNAP1 (Daniel et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to Daniel et al., 2018.

claim: Both Cockayne syndrome proteins (CSA and CSB) are implicated in repair of UV lesions on active rDNA.
source: Notably, both Cockayne syndrome proteins (CSA and CSB) are implicated in this specific repair reaction, as well as the UV-stimulated scaffold protein A (UVSSA), a protein required for the stabilization of CSB specifically after UV irradiation (Higa et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to Daniel et al., 2018 and Higa et al., 2016.

claim: UVSSA is a protein required for the stabilization of CSB specifically after UV irradiation.
source: Notably, both Cockayne syndrome proteins (CSA and CSB) are implicated in this specific repair reaction, as well as the UV-stimulated scaffold protein A (UVSSA), a protein required for the stabilization of CSB specifically after UV irradiation (Higa et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to Higa et al., 2016.

claim: The S9.6 antibody can recognize other nucleic acid structures besides DNA:RNA hybrids in immunofluorescence assay.
source: However, a careful interpretation of these results should be made because a recent paper demonstrates that the S9.6 antibody, specific for DNA:RNA hybrids, can also recognize other nucleic acid structures in immunofluorescence assay (Smolka et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citation to Smolka et al., 2021.

claim: The S9.6 signal is prominently cytoplasmic and nucleolar and derives mainly from ribosomal RNA.
source: It has been demonstrated that the S9.6 signal is prominently cytoplasmic and nucleolar and derives mainly from ribosomal RNA (Smolka et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citation to Smolka et al., 2021.

claim: XAB2 intervenes in the early steps of TC-NER or at least in the steps that imply the activity of CSB and TFIIH.
source: These results suggest that XAB2 intervenes in the early steps of TC-NER or at least in the steps that imply the activity of CSB and TFIIH and most probably the early RNAP2 blocking-recognition step.
evidence: Inferred from PLA data showing XAB2 release from CSA and XPG but not from CSB or XPB (Figure 6), combined with knowledge of TC-NER pathway steps.

claim: XAB2 most probably functions in the early RNAP2 blocking-recognition step.
source: These results suggest that XAB2 intervenes in the early steps of TC-NER or at least in the steps that imply the activity of CSB and TFIIH and most probably the early RNAP2 blocking-recognition step.
evidence: Inferred from data showing RNAP2 remains longer on UV lesions in XAB2-silenced cells (Figure 7B), suggesting XAB2 helps RNAP2 detach from lesions during damage recognition.

claim: XAB2 is released from CSA and XPG proteins associated with R-loops processing.
source: However, the reduction of interactions between XAB2 and CSA or XPG is less striking than the one with R-loops. As suggested in Goulielmaki et al., 2021, another working hypothesis would be that XAB2 is released from CSA and XPG proteins associated with R-loops processing.
evidence: Inferred from PLA data showing XAB2 release from both R-loops (Figure 5D) and from CSA/XPG (Figure 6A, C), combined with citation to Goulielmaki et al., 2021.

claim: The binding between XAB2 and its substrate is not restored in TCR-deficient cells.
source: Moreover, in CSA−/− and CSB−/− cell lines, in which UV lesions on transcribed strands of genes are not repaired, the amount of XAB2 immunoprecipitated remained high all along the time course of the experiment (3 and 16 hr) (Figure 5A). These results hinted that the binding between XAB2 and its substrate is not restored in TCR-deficient cells.
evidence: Inferred from immunoprecipitation data showing sustained high XAB2 immunoprecipitation in CSA/CSB mutant cells (Figure 5A), suggesting altered XAB2-substrate dynamics when repair is defective.

claim: The re-establishment of the proper localization of XAB2 within the nucleus after the DNA repair process depends either on the repair process per se or on the restart of transcription after the achievement of DNA repair reactions.
source: However, this release persisted 16 hr after UV-C exposure (Figure 3C blue and red curves compared to black curve and Figure 3—figure supplement 4), suggesting that the re-establishment of the proper localization of XAB2 within the nucleus after the DNA repair process depends either on the repair process per se or on the restart of transcription after the achievement of DNA repair reactions.
evidence: Inferred from data showing XAB2 localization is not restored in CSA/CSB mutant cells where repair and transcription restart are defective (Figure 3C).

claim: The increased XAB2 mobility might partly be explained by the release of XAB2 from its substrate R-loops and its partner CSA and XPG.
source: In conclusion, we describe here an increased mobility of the protein XAB2 during the DNA damage-dependent transcription inhibition. This increased mobility might partly be explained by the release of XAB2 from its substrate R-loops and its partner CSA and XPG.
evidence: Supported by FRAP data showing increased XAB2 mobility (Figure 4A), PLA data showing XAB2 release from R-loops (Figure 5D), and release from CSA and XPG (Figure 6A, C).

claim: The absence of XAB2 hinders the overall transcription activity of the cells.
source: Importantly, we demonstrate that XAB2 plays an anchoring role for RNAP2 to its substrate during transcription and helps RNAP2 to detach from UV lesions after DNA damage. As aconsequence, the absence of XAB2 hinders the overall transcription activity of the cells and severely affects the TC-NER capacity (Figure 8).
evidence: Supported by RRS data showing no transcription restart in XAB2-silenced cells (Figure 1C) and FRAP data showing increased RNAP2 mobility in XAB2-silenced cells (Figure 7A).

claim: The absence of XAB2 severely affects the TC-NER capacity.
source: Importantly, we demonstrate that XAB2 plays an anchoring role for RNAP2 to its substrate during transcription and helps RNAP2 to detach from UV lesions after DNA damage. As aconsequence, the absence of XAB2 hinders the overall transcription activity of the cells and severely affects the TC-NER capacity (Figure 8).
evidence: Supported by TCR-UDS data showing decreased repair replication in XAB2-silenced cells (Figure 1D) and PLA data showing prolonged RNAP2-lesion interaction in XAB2-silenced cells (Figure 7B).

claim: XAB2 helps RNAP2 to detach from UV lesions after DNA damage.
source: Importantly, we demonstrate that XAB2 plays an anchoring role for RNAP2 to its substrate during transcription and helps RNAP2 to detach from UV lesions after DNA damage.
evidence: Supported by PLA data showing stronger and more persistent RNAP2-6-4PP interaction in XAB2-silenced cells (Figure 7B), indicating RNAP2 remains stuck on lesions without XAB2.

claim: NER requires more than 30 different proteins that are recruited sequentially to the DNA damage site.
source: In mammals, the different steps of NER require more than 30 different proteins that are recruited sequentially to the DNA damage site, as demonstrated by the different studies of NER proteins kinetics (Moné et al., 2004; Politi et al., 2005; Rademakers et al., 2003; van den Boom et al., 2004; Zotter et al., 2006).
evidence: Supported by citations to multiple studies on NER protein kinetics.

claim: The first step of NER consists of damage recognition, followed by the opening of the DNA duplex, dual incisions on both sides of the damage, excision of 24–32 oligonucleotides containing the damage and, finally, gap-filling by repair DNA synthesis.
source: The first step of NER consists of damage recognition, followed by the opening of the DNA duplex, dual incisions on both sides of the damage, excision of 24–32 oligonucleotides containing the damage and, finally, gap-filling by repair DNA synthesis.
evidence: Represents established knowledge about NER pathway steps.

claim: NER is divided into two subpathways: Global Genome repair (GG-NER) and Transcription-Coupled repair (TC-NER).
source: NER is divided into two subpathways depending on DNA lesions position within the genome. The Global Genome repair (GG-NER) will detect and repair lesions throughout the genome, whereas Transcription-Coupled repair (TC-NER) is associated with RNA polymerase 2 (RNAP2) to repair lesions on the transcribed strand of active genes (Marteijn et al., 2014).
evidence: Represents established knowledge about NER subpathways, supported by citation to Marteijn et al., 2014.

claim: TC-NER is associated with RNA polymerase 2 (RNAP2) to repair lesions on the transcribed strand of active genes.
source: The Global Genome repair (GG-NER) will detect and repair lesions throughout the genome, whereas Transcription-Coupled repair (TC-NER) is associated with RNA polymerase 2 (RNAP2) to repair lesions on the transcribed strand of active genes (Marteijn et al., 2014).
evidence: Represents established knowledge about TC-NER, supported by citation to Marteijn et al., 2014.

claim: CS and TTD patients are not cancer prone but present severe neurological and developmental features.
source: Importantly, CS and TTD patients are not cancer prone but present severe neurological and developmental features (Hanawalt, 1994).
evidence: Represents established clinical knowledge about CS and TTD, supported by citation to Hanawalt, 1994.

claim: XAB2 protein consists of 15 tetratricopeptide repeat (TPR) motifs that carry out protein–protein interactions.
source: Xeroderma Pigmentosum group A (XPA)-binding protein 2 (XAB2) is a highly conserved protein of 100 kDa and consists of 15 tetratricopeptide repeat (TPR) motifs that carry out protein–protein interactions.
evidence: Represents established structural knowledge about XAB2 protein.

claim: R-loops are a three-stranded nucleic acid structure composed of a DNA:RNA hybrid and the associated nontemplate single-stranded DNA.
source: Interestingly, AQR has a role in removing R-loops, a three-stranded nucleic acids structure composed of a DNA:RNA hybrid and the associated nontemplate single-stranded DNA (Sollier et al., 2014).
evidence: Represents established knowledge about R-loop structure.

claim: R-loops can form during transcription, when an RNA molecule emerging from the transcription machinery hybridizes with its DNA template.
source: These structures can form during transcription, when an RNA molecule emerging from the transcription machinery hybridizes with its DNA template.
evidence: Represents established knowledge about R-loop formation mechanism.

claim: Transcription blockage due to DNA damage appears to result in R-loops formation.
source: Transcription blockage due to DNA damage appears to result in R-loops formation (Mullenders, 2015; Steurer and Marteijn, 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to Mullenders, 2015 and Steurer and Marteijn, 2017.

claim: The mobility of late-stage spliceosomes changes after UV irradiation and depends on DDR signaling pathways.
source: As for XAB2, the mobility of the late-stage spliceosomes changes after UV irradiation. This mobilization depends on DDR signaling pathways (Tresini et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to Tresini et al., 2015.

claim: ATM and ATR kinases are key mediators of DDR, which induce cell cycle arrest and facilitate DNA repair.
source: Key mediators of DDR are the ATM and ATR kinases, which induce cell cycle arrest and facilitate DNA repair.
evidence: Represents established knowledge about DDR signaling.
